Talkers
tawk'ers
n. pl. (those given to speech; in Titus, the vain talkers whose religion is words without works)
From talk, of Germanic origin. Titus 1:10 renders the Greek mataiologos — from mataios (empty, futile) and logos (word) — an empty-word man, one whose speech carries nothing.

Biblical Definition

“For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision” (Titus 1:10). The three nouns build: unruly, meaning not subject to the order of the church; vain talkers, whose words are hollow; deceivers, which is what hollow words become when they are believed. The next verse gives their effect and their motive — they subvert whole houses for filthy lucre's sake — so this is not a complaint about men who talk too much but about a ministry of empty speech that does real damage. Paul warns Timothy about the same pattern in another form: younger widows “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” (1 Timothy 5:13). Ezekiel supplies the Old Testament use, where the talkers are outside and the covenant people are their subject: Israel is “taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people” (Ezekiel 36:3). The chapter that follows that indictment is the promise of a new heart and a new spirit — God's answer to the reproach is not a better reputation but a changed people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a talker as one who talks, and especially a loquacious person, a prattler, a boaster of what he will do.

expand to see more

TALKER, n. One who talks; also, a loquacious person, male or female; a prattler.

2. A boaster; a braggart; used by Shakespeare, but not now so applied.

VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance.

TATTLER, n. One who tattles; an idle talker; one who tells tales.

BUSYBODY, n. One who officiously concerns himself with the affairs of others; a meddling person.

Key Scripture

Titus 1:10 — "For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision:"

Titus 1:11 — "Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake."

1 Timothy 5:13 — "And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not."

Ezekiel 36:3 — "Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people:"

Modern Corruption

The church has built its platforms on the very gift Scripture treats with suspicion, and fluency now passes for faithfulness.

expand to see more

Scripture is markedly unimpressed by verbal facility. Titus 1:10 puts vain talkers among the unruly and the deceivers; James warns that not many should be masters, knowing they receive the greater condemnation; and Paul reminds the Corinthians that the kingdom of God is not in word but in power. The modern arrangement runs the other way: influence follows the microphone, and the men most heard are those most able to talk. A ministry is not tested by the size of its audience or the quality of its phrases but by whether the households under it are being built up or quietly overturned. Fluency is a gift and it is not a qualification; the list in Titus 1 requires a man's life, and asks only that he be apt to teach.

1 Timothy 5:13 names the domestic form, and it should be read without the condescension it usually receives. Paul's concern is idleness turning into speech that circulates through households doing harm — and the same pattern operates now with far greater reach, in a congregation where anyone may broadcast to everyone. The biblical categories here are plain ones: talebearing, meddling, speaking things which they ought not. They are sins of the tongue, they wreck churches, and the remedy Paul gives is not silence but useful work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek mataiologos (G3151), a vain talker — Titus 1:10, its only occurrence; phluaros (G5397), a tattler — 1 Timothy 5:13.

expand to see more

Greek mataiologos (G3151) — an empty talker; Titus 1:10, its only occurrence in the New Testament.

Greek mataiologia (G3150) — vain jangling; 1 Timothy 1:6, of those who turned aside from charity out of a pure heart.

Greek anupotaktos (G506) — unruly, not subject; Titus 1:10, and Titus 1:6 of children who must not be so.

Greek phluaros (G5397) — a babbler, tattler; 1 Timothy 5:13, its only occurrence.

Ezekiel 36:3 shows the covenant people as the subject of the talkers, and Ezekiel 36:26 gives God's answer — a new heart.

Usage

"“Many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers” — the three nouns build on one another."

"“Tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” — the domestic form."

"Fluency is a gift; it was never a qualification."
